title: How do I write that in Rayner?
answer: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees

checks.question: Run the code-edits recipe twice in one step: count += 1 becomes count += 2, then count += 3, each morph with markAdded. What does a reader who opens that step from a link see, and is there any sign of count += 2?
checks.answer: Two lines, let count = 0 and count += 3, with count += 3 marked as added. The second morph fades count += 2 out along with its mark, so nothing in the resting picture shows that it existed; to keep it, draw the earlier panel beside the result, as the before panels on this page do.

checks.question: In the camera scenario, the author also enters a second circle at (5, 0) before calling s.focus(subject). Is it in the result picture, and where is it?
checks.answer: It is out of the picture. The closer view frames 6 of the stage’s 16 units around the first circle, roughly x = −3 to 3, so a circle at x = 5 falls outside it. It is still at (5, 0), because s.focus moves only the camera, and s.focus(‘all’) would bring it back into view.

checks.question: An author wants the chart scenario to plot numbers that each reader types into a box. Can a Rayner page do that, and what can the author offer instead?
checks.answer: No. A reader can only choose among the options a setting declares, and the build makes one scenario per option before anyone reads the page. The author can declare a setting whose options are a few prepared data sets, so each one is a scenario the build makes and the author can read.

steps.title: How do I give an idea its own link and picture?
steps.line: Predict: what address would a link to this step end with?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. this.step opens a step with a name, a title and a caption. Whatever the lines after it enter becomes that step’s resting picture, and the step’s name becomes part of its address.

steps.title: An empty step, then the greeting
steps.line: This picture and its caption are all a reader gets from a link ending ?step=hello.
steps.caption: A link ending ?step=hello opens the finished greeting without playing its entry, so this resting picture and its caption carry everything a direct visitor gets. The empty frame on the left is a separate drawing of the step before entry, not something these lines draw.

steps.title: How do I let a reader switch between prepared scenarios?
steps.line: Predict: which scenario is this page showing, and how many did the build make?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. static settings declares an option list, the build makes one scenario for every option, and settingsOf(this) tells construct which scenario it is building. The two options shown are excerpts from this page’s own feature picker.

steps.title: The default scenario, then the scenario you chose
steps.line: The default scenario is Animations; this page is the Settings scenario.
steps.caption: The left card names the default scenario and the right card this one, with the number of scenarios the build made: one per option in the feature picker. Choosing a feature switches between those prepared scenarios; it does not run the scene on new input.
steps.picture: Before: the default scenario, feature = animation; 1 labelled value; 2 labelled values.

steps.title: How do I trace a path through a flowchart?
steps.line: Predict: once the walk ends, what stays on the flowchart?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. s.show draws a diagram from geometry captured at build time. d.walk sends a token along an edge that exists in the diagram, here Start → Finish; trail: true is the walk option this scenario is about.

steps.title: A bare flowchart, then its walked edge marked
steps.line: The trail stays on Start → Finish after the walk ends.
steps.caption: The trail stays on Start → Finish after the token has gone, so the route can be inspected at rest, and it follows the captured edge rather than a shortcut. The unmarked copy on the left is a separate drawing of the flowchart before the walk.
steps.picture: Flowchart: 2 nodes, 1 link; Before: the captured flowchart, no path marked; Flowchart: 2 nodes, 1 link. Travelled: Start → Finish.

steps.title: How do I point at one line of code?
steps.line: Predict: once the focus ends, is any line still marked?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. s.code draws the lines as a code panel. block.focus(1, {as: 'update'}) points at the line with index 1, the second, and says why.

steps.title: Two plain lines, then the second marked as the update
steps.line: The update bar stays on count += 1 after the motion stops.
steps.caption: The update bar stays on count += 1 after the focus finishes, which ties the caption to the line it explains. The plain copy on the left is a separate drawing of the panel before the focus.
steps.picture: Before: the two lines, nothing marked; Code, 2 lines; Code, 2 lines. Update: 2: count += 1.

steps.title: How do I show an edit without redrawing the code?
steps.line: Predict: after the morph, which line carries the added mark?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. block.morph turns the panel into a new list of lines and keeps the lines both versions share in place; markAdded: true marks what the edit introduced.

steps.title: count += 1 edited to count += 2, the new line marked
steps.line: Only count += 2 carries the added mark; let count = 0 kept its place.
steps.caption: let count = 0 stays where it was, and count += 2 replaces the old increment and carries the mark. The mark labels the current line; it is not a history of earlier edits. The panel on the left is a separate drawing of the version before the morph.
steps.picture: Before: count += 1; Code, 2 lines; Code, 2 lines. Added: 2: count += 2.

steps.title: How do I animate a patch I already have?
steps.line: Predict: which line does the patch let travel whole, and which does it rewrite?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. parseUnifiedDiff reads a patch, as Git prints one, into hunks. TransformDiff takes its pairing from those hunks, so the motion can show only the change the patch contains.

steps.title: n += 1, then n += 2 as the patch says
steps.line: let n = 0 kept its place, and the line the hunk changes was rewritten.
steps.caption: The hunk keeps let n = 0 as context, so that line travelled whole, and pairs the removed n += 1 with the added n += 2, which kept n += and swapped the number. Under the result, diffLines, which diffs the two versions itself, finds the same removed and added line; the patch also carries let n = 0 as context. The code on the left is a separate drawing of the version before.
steps.picture: Before: the code with n += 1; After: let n = 0; then n += 2;; Under the code: the patch's operations, = - +, and diffLines', - +.

steps.title: How do I show one shape turning into another?
steps.line: Predict: opened from a link, do these lines leave the circle, the square or both?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. Transform reshapes the object already on stage, point by point, until it matches the target.

steps.title: A circle before, the square it became after
steps.line: From a link, these lines leave a square; the circle is a separate drawing.
steps.caption: Only the square comes from the recipe: Transform turned the circle into it. The circle on the left is a separate drawing of the starting shape, so a direct visitor can inspect the change without seeing it play.
steps.picture: Before: a circle; After: the circle has become a square.

steps.title: How do I change a label and keep its shared letters?
steps.line: Predict: from cache miss to cache hit, which letters move rather than fade?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. TransformMatchingText pairs equal characters between the two texts, moves each pair and fades the characters left over. s.keep tells the stage that the new text stays.

steps.title: cache miss becomes cache hit
steps.line: The shared letters slid into place, and the others faded.
steps.caption: The lists under the result record the pairs the animation used. Matching follows characters, not words, so a letter can move into a different word. The smaller cache miss on the left is a separate drawing of the text before the change.

matched.moved: c a c h e i

after.moved: c a c h e i

steps.picture: Before: cache miss; Under cache hit: the letters moved, c a c h e i; faded in, h t; faded out, m s s; 1 label.

steps.title: How do I reorder items so each one travels to its new place?
steps.line: Predict: when A B C becomes C A B, does each tile slide, or does each letter change in place?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. Each tile carries a key. TransformMatching with matchByKey pairs tiles by key, not by position, so tile C travels from last to first.

steps.title: A B C, then C A B with each tile moved whole
steps.line: Each tile travelled to its new place; none changed its letter.
steps.caption: Pairing by key moved C from the end to the front and A and B one place on. Transform pairs by position, and would have morphed the first tile’s A into C where it stood. The row on the left is a separate drawing of the order before the move.
steps.picture: Before: the tiles in the order A, B, C; After: the tiles in the order C, A, B, each moved whole.

steps.title: How do I make a new shape from one and keep the original?
steps.line: Predict: once the copy has morphed, how many shapes are left?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. TransformFromCopy morphs a copy of the source into the result, so the source stays where it is and the scene keeps the result.

steps.title: One square, then the square and the circle made from its copy
steps.line: Both shapes remain: the square, and the circle its copy became.
steps.caption: Transform would have turned the square itself into the circle; TransformFromCopy morphed a copy, so the square stays and the circle sits beside it. The left panel is a separate drawing of the square alone.
steps.picture: Before: the square alone; After: the square, unchanged; After: a circle beside the square, morphed from its copy.

steps.title: How do I put an object back after a demonstration?
steps.line: Predict: opened from a link, would these lines show that the circle ever moved?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. saveState() records the circle’s points and style. Restore animates the circle back to that record from wherever the lines in between moved it.

steps.title: The circle moves away and returns to its saved place
steps.line: Without the dashed outline, the resting picture would hide the circle’s trip.
steps.caption: Restore brought the circle back to the place saveState() recorded, so the circle alone gives no sign that it moved. The dashed outline, which this page draws separately, marks where it went before Restore.
steps.picture: Before: a circle whose state is saved; After: the circle is back at its saved place; a dashed outline marks where it moved to; A dashed outline where the circle moved to before Restore.

steps.title: How do I write a word in, letter by letter?
steps.line: Predict: opened from a link, does a written word look any different from one that faded in?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. Write draws each letter’s outline and then fills it, each letter starting before the one before it finishes. s.keep puts the word in the stage’s description.

steps.title: An empty panel, then the written word
steps.line: At rest, a written word looks like any other word.
steps.caption: Write changes how the letters arrive, not where they end: at rest the word is the same Rayner a fade would leave, and a link to this step shows no sign of the writing. When the order of writing is the lesson, draw that order, as this tour draws its before panels.
steps.picture: Before: an empty panel, nothing written yet; After: the word Rayner, written.

steps.title: How do I send something along a curved route?
steps.line: Predict: once the move ends, where is the token, and is the route still drawn?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. ArcBetweenPoints draws a circular arc from one point to another, bending through angle, here a quarter turn. MoveAlongPath carries the token along that path instead of in a straight line.

steps.title: A token at the start, then at the end of its curved route
steps.line: The token rests at the route’s far end, and the route stays drawn.
steps.caption: MoveAlongPath followed the arc, so the token travelled the curve rather than the straight line between its ends, and it rests at the far end of the route. The route is still drawn because the recipe entered it; the motion leaves no trail of its own. The left panel is a separate drawing of the token at the start.
steps.picture: Before: the token at the start of its route; After: a curved route dipping below the straight line between its ends, with the token at its far end.

steps.title: How do I choose how a move speeds up and slows down?
steps.line: Predict: which dot arrives at full speed, and which comes back to where it started?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. rateFunc maps the time a play has run to how far along its move is: smooth eases in and out, rushInto starts slow and arrives at full speed, rushFrom leaves at full speed and eases out, and thereAndBack goes out and comes back.

steps.title: Four rate functions, each move marked at each tenth of its run
steps.line: Wide gaps are fast: rushInto at its end, rushFrom at its start.
steps.caption: Each tick marks where a dot was after another tenth of its run, read from the same rate function, so wide gaps mean speed: rushInto’s ticks spread out as it arrives, rushFrom’s as it leaves, smooth’s in the middle, and thereAndBack’s dot is back where it started. The bare tracks on the left are a separate drawing, before any move.
steps.picture: Before: four bare tracks, each dot at its start; After: four tracks, each with ticks where its dot was at every tenth of its run; smooth’s dot is at its end, rushInto’s dot is at its end, rushFrom’s dot is at its end, thereAndBack’s dot is at its start.

steps.title: How do I make a result stand out after the motion ends?
steps.line: Predict: when Circumscribe ends, is anything still drawn round 42?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. Circumscribe animates an outline round its target; keep: true is the option this scenario is about, and s.keep gives the outline a description for readers who cannot see it.

steps.title: A plain 42, then 42 left in a box
steps.line: The box round 42 is still drawn once the motion ends.
steps.caption: Circumscribe normally removes its outline when the animation ends. keep: true leaves the box round 42, and the description says what it marks. The plain 42 on the left is a separate drawing.
steps.picture: Before: the result 42, unmarked; After: the result 42 remains in a box; 1 label.

steps.title: How do I single out one value in a row?
steps.line: Predict: what does the underline span, and do the other values move?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. Underline draws a stroke just under its target’s box, left to right. The other values are not touched.

steps.title: Three values, then the middle one underlined
steps.line: 42 is underlined, and the row has not moved.
steps.caption: The underline is as wide as 42 and sits just under it, so it singles out one value without boxing it or moving its neighbours, and its description says which. The row on the left is a separate drawing, before the mark.
steps.picture: Before: the values 12, 42 and 7, none marked; After: 42 is underlined; 12 and 7 are not; 3 labels.

steps.title: How do I show that several things count as one span?
steps.line: Predict: which way does the brace’s tip point, and what sits past it?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. Brace draws a curly bracket along one side of its target’s box: [0, -1] puts it underneath, its tip pointing down. putAtTip places anything just past the tip.

steps.title: Four letters, then a brace that counts them
steps.line: The brace spans all four letters, and 4 items sits past its tip.
steps.caption: The brace is as wide as the row’s box, so it takes the four letters together, and putAtTip set 4 items just past its tip. A brace is built once from the box: if the row moves later, the brace stays where it was. The row on the left is a separate drawing, before the brace.
steps.picture: Before: the letters a b c d; After: a brace under all four letters, its tip pointing at 4 items; 1 label.

steps.title: How do I bring the reader closer to a small subject?
steps.line: Predict: after the focus, has the circle moved, or has the view?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. s.focus frames a subject for the reader, with a margin round it; s.focus('all') returns to the whole stage.

steps.title: The same circle, seen through a closer view
steps.line: The view moved in; the circle kept its coordinates.
steps.caption: The ruler, which this page draws across the whole stage, now shows only its middle, while the circle is still at (0, 0): the view moved, not the circle. A before panel would sit inside the same closer view, so the ruler is the reference instead.
steps.picture: A circle at the centre of a ruler that spans the stage from −7 to 7, numbered on its even ticks; The camera now frames 6.0 of the stage’s 16 units; the circle is still at (0, 0) with radius 0.6.

steps.title: How do I plot the model’s numbers?
steps.line: Predict: which values does the line pass through?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. Axes maps data coordinates to stage positions, and lineGraph joins the points you give it through that mapping.

steps.title: Three values as numbers, then as a line on axes
steps.line: The line passes through 0, 2 and 1, each placed by the axes.
steps.caption: The axes placed each point, so the line can be checked against the numbers without guessing where an author drew it by hand. The card on the left is a separate drawing of the same values.
steps.picture: Before: the model’s three values as numbers; 3 labelled values; After: a line through values zero, two and one at x zero, one and two.

steps.title: How do I place a value on a scale?
steps.line: Predict: 7 has no tick of its own, so where does the dot go?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. NumberLine draws a scale from its range, with a tick at each step; n2p turns a number into the point where it belongs on the line.

steps.title: The value 7, then 7 placed on a scale from 0 to 10
steps.line: The dot sits between the ticks for 6 and 8, where n2p put 7.
steps.caption: n2p measured 7 along the line, so the dot sits between the ticks for 6 and 8 with no position typed by hand, and it would stay right if the line moved or scaled. The number on the left is a separate drawing of the value.
steps.picture: Before: the value 7, on no scale; After: a scale from 0 to 10, ticked every 2, with a dot at 7, between the ticks for 6 and 8.

steps.title: How do I compare values on one scale?
steps.line: Predict: how long is MRU’s bar beside LRU’s?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. bars, from the drawing kit, draws each row on one scale with aligned starts, here a maximum of 4, so the lengths compare directly.

steps.title: Two counts, then the same counts as bars on one scale
steps.line: MRU’s bar is a third as long as LRU’s, both measured from one start.
steps.caption: Both bars start at one edge and share the scale of 4, so 1 hit draws a third as long as 3 hits and the comparison needs no reading of numbers. Each label and value is keyed, so a later picture can morph the same rows. The card on the left is a separate drawing of the same counts.
steps.picture: Before: the counts as numbers; 2 labelled values; After: two bars on one scale of 4, LRU at 3 hits and MRU at 1 hit, a third as long.

steps.title: How do I count a number up to a new value?
steps.line: Predict: between 0 and 12.5, does the number fade across or count through the values in between?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. DecimalNumber is a Text that keeps its value. A Transform to another DecimalNumber counts through the values in between, with the decimals and suffix it was given.

steps.title: 0.0 ms before, 12.5 ms after
steps.line: From a link the number reads 12.5 ms; the count happened in between.
steps.caption: Transform interpolated the value, so a reader watching saw 0.0 ms climb through the values in between to 12.5 ms, and one opening the link sees 12.5 ms alone. The 0.0 ms on the left is a separate drawing of where the count started.
steps.picture: Before: the count at 0.0 ms; After: the count reads 12.5 ms.

steps.title: How do I keep a label in step with the model’s state?
steps.line: Predict: after the sync, what number does the label show, and where does it come from?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. this.state holds values the model decides. view builds a label from that state, and label.sync() rebuilds the label after the state changes.

steps.title: state.count goes from 0 to 1, and the label follows
steps.line: Label and trace both read 1, because the view rebuilt the label from state.
steps.caption: Setting count alone changes nothing on screen; sync rebuilt the label from count, so the label and the recorded state both read 1. The 0 on the left is a separate drawing of the view before the change.
steps.picture: Before: the view of state.count = 0; Recorded count: 1; 1 label.

steps.title: How do I name a point in the picture?
steps.line: Predict: what does the pin say, and where does it point?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. s.pin puts a label at a point in the picture and draws a leader to it.

steps.title: A bare circle, then its centre pinned
steps.line: The word centre sits at the end of a leader to the circle’s centre.
steps.caption: The leader ties the word centre to the circle’s centre, so the label names a place without another animation. The bare circle on the left is a separate drawing.
steps.picture: Before: a circle, nothing named; After: a circle whose centre is pinned; A pin marked “centre”.

steps.title: How do I lay out panels for a right-to-left page?
steps.line: Predict: in a right-to-left stage, where does a card placed at start go?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. direction: 'rtl' lays the stage’s logical regions out right to left. The card’s own direction: 'ltr' sets the order of the text inside it.

steps.title: Start, in a left-to-right stage and in this right-to-left one
steps.line: Start is on the right in this stage, yet the card still reads Count, 3.
steps.caption: The card sits on the right, the start of a right-to-left stage, yet still reads Count, 3: placement and the order inside the card are separate choices. The outline on the left marks where start would be in a left-to-right stage.
steps.picture: Before: an outline on the left, where start is in a left-to-right stage; 1 labelled value; 1 label.

steps.title: How do I colour a scene that has no diagram?
steps.line: Predict: which colours change with the palette: the card, the heading, or both?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. palette('nord') gives the stage a named palette of paper, ink and accent. The stage’s helpers colour from it, and s.palette, s.emphasis and s.soft hand the same colours to what you draw.

steps.title: This tour’s usual colours, then the same stage in nord
steps.line: Paper, heading and card all took nord’s colours from one option.
steps.caption: One option recoloured the paper, the heading and the card, and the card lists the colours s.palette gave it, so a drawing coloured from s.palette follows a change of palette and keeps its contrast. The panel on the left is a separate drawing in github-dark, this tour’s usual palette.
steps.picture: Before: a panel in github-dark, the tour’s usual paper and ink; “palette('nord')”, 3 labelled values.

steps.title: How do I set a formula?
steps.line: Predict: does the page typeset the formula when it loads, or carry it ready-made?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. lettering: {math: true} asks the build for maths, and MathTex draws TeX as outlines, typeset once when rayner snapshots runs. describe says the formula in words, because outlines have no text to read.

steps.title: The TeX an author writes, then the formula it sets
steps.line: The page draws stored outlines; the browser typesets nothing.
steps.caption: rayner snapshots typeset a^2+b^2=c^2 once and stored its outlines in scene.lettering.json, so the page draws them and runs no TeX. The description gives the formula in words for readers who cannot see it. The source on the left is a separate drawing, as the author types it.
steps.picture: Before: the TeX source a^2+b^2=c^2; After: the formula a squared plus b squared equals c squared, typeset.

steps.title: How do I reveal a line as if drawn by hand?
steps.line: Predict: opened from a link, what is left of the pen’s motion?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. s.sketch reveals a path along its length with a tool riding its tip, and describe says what the finished stroke shows.

steps.title: Two end points, then the line the pen drew between them
steps.line: Of the pen’s motion, only the finished line is left at rest.
steps.caption: The pen disappears when drawing ends, and the rising line remains; its description carries the same fact to readers who do not see the motion. The two dots on the left are a separate drawing of the path’s ends.
steps.picture: Before: the path’s two ends, nothing drawn; After: a rising line, drawn.

steps.title: How do I turn a globe to face another place?
steps.line: Predict: once the turn ends, where is London on the globe?
steps.caption: Each feature takes a few lines of the scene, and the picture they leave at rest is what a reader who opens the step from a link sees. seenFrom draws a 3D model through a viewpoint as flat, keyed pieces, and between interpolates two viewpoints. Follow redraws the globe from one number on each frame, so the turn passes through the viewpoints in between.

steps.title: The globe from the Atlantic, then turned to face London
steps.line: London now faces the reader, turned by one number from 0 to 1.
steps.caption: Follow drew the globe from between(a, b, t) on each frame, so parts turning away went behind the globe instead of sliding across its face, and from a link the reader sees the end of the turn: London near the middle. The globe on the left is a separate drawing from the first viewpoint.
steps.picture: Before: the globe from the Atlantic, London near its right edge; After: the globe, turned to face London, which sits near its middle; 1 label.
